record.original_question: As an intermediate step toward polynomial-time proper learning of decision trees, can one efficiently learn the target using a hypothesis class that is more expressive than decision trees but still retains their desirable interpretability properties, such as branching programs or generalized decision trees whose internal nodes branch on halfspace outcomes?

evidence.quote: As an intermediate step towards such an algorithm, one could consider allowing the algorithm return more expressive hypotheses that nevertheless share the desirability of decision trees (e.g. interpretability).

Two concrete examples are branching programs-generalizations of decision trees where the underlying graph is a DAG-and generalized decision trees whose internal nodes branch on the outcomes of halfspaces instead of singleton variables.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. A decision tree over $\{0,1\}^n$ is a rooted binary tree whose internal nodes are labeled by input variables $x_i$ and whose leaves are labeled by $\{0,1\}$; on input $x$, one routes from the root by branching on the labeled variable at each internal node and outputs the leaf label reached. A learning algorithm for a concept class $\mathcal{C}$ is called proper if its hypothesis is itself a member of $\mathcal{C}$. It is a well-known open problem whether the class of size-$s$ decision trees is properly PAC learnable in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,s,1/\varepsilon)$ under the uniform distribution on $\{0,1\}^n$ (with membership queries allowed).

Two natural, more expressive hypothesis classes that retain the interpretability of decision trees are:

(i) Branching programs: rooted directed acyclic graphs in which each internal (non-sink) node is labeled by a variable $x_i$ and has two outgoing edges labeled $0$ and $1$; sinks are labeled by $\{0,1\}$. Evaluation proceeds analogously to a decision tree.

(ii) Generalized decision trees with halfspace queries: rooted binary trees in which each internal node is labeled by a halfspace $\mathrm{sign}(\langle w, x\rangle - \theta)$ (rather than a single coordinate), with $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, and leaves are labeled by $\{0,1\}$.

Problem. Design a learning algorithm with the following guarantee, or prove that none exists under standard complexity assumptions: given $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and access (e.g., via uniform random examples and/or membership queries) to an unknown size-$s$ decision tree $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, output, in time $\mathrm{poly}(n, s, 1/\varepsilon)$, a hypothesis $h$ that is either a branching program or a generalized decision tree with halfspace queries (of size $\mathrm{poly}(n,s,1/\varepsilon)$), such that $\Pr_{x \sim \{0,1\}^n}[h(x) \neq f(x)] \le \varepsilon$.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem accompanying a result giving an n^{O(log log n)}-time algorithm for properly learning decision trees under the uniform distribution with membership queries. No polynomial-time proper algorithm — nor a polynomial-time algorithm using the suggested intermediate hypothesis classes (branching programs or halfspace-branching generalized decision trees) — appears to have been reported in subsequent literature.

status_evidence.title: Open Problem: Properly learning decision trees in polynomial time?
status_evidence.snippet: Open problem regarding polynomial-time proper learning of decision trees, with intermediate milestones suggested.
status_evidence.claim: Polynomial-time proper learning of decision trees is open; intermediate hypotheses are suggested.

status_evidence.title: Properly learning decision trees in almost polynomial time
status_evidence.snippet: Provides an n^{O(log log n)}-time membership-query algorithm for properly learning decision trees under uniform distribution.
status_evidence.claim: Best current bound is quasipolynomial (n^{O(log log n)}), not polynomial.
